The paper studies electromagnetic invisibility cloaks obtained by high order transformations from general anisotropic media.
It proves that for any incident plane wave at any frequency, the scattered wave is identically zero.
The scattering matrix for finite energy wave packets is the identity operator.
Multiple spherical cloaks can be located at different points in space without intersecting.
The cloaked objects are completely decoupled from the exterior electromagnetic fields.
Electromagnetic waves inside the cloaked region cannot leave, and waves outside cannot enter the concealed region.
The tangential components of electric and magnetic fields vanish at the boundary of the cloaked objects.
Von Neumann’s method of self-adjoint extensions is used to handle singularities in the permittivity and permeability at the cloak boundary.
The transformation used blows up a point into a spherical shell, creating the cloaking layer.
Permittivity and permeability tensors become degenerate at the boundary of the cloaked region.
The analysis assumes non-dispersive media, valid over narrow frequency ranges.
The cloaks can cloak both passive and active devices inside the concealed region.
The paper generalizes previous results that considered only first order transformations and isotropic media.
The electromagnetic fields and material tensors transform as tensor densities under the coordinate transformation.
The operator defining Maxwell’s equations in the cloaking medium is essentially self-adjoint, ensuring unique finite-energy solutions.
The cloaking function g(ρ) used in the transformation is twice continuously differentiable and strictly increasing between the inner radius a and outer radius b.
The paper defines precise functional spaces and domains for the electromagnetic fields to rigorously formulate the problem.
The cloaking transformation is identity outside the outer radius b, ensuring no alteration of fields there.
The cloaking results apply to general anisotropic materials, including crystals.
The paper uses a Schrödinger-type formulation of Maxwell’s equations to analyze the problem.
